note: Consensus recommendations from over 200 stakeholders on validation, certification and national safety reporting.
title: Toward a responsible future: recommendations for AI-enabled clinical decision support
journal: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association

reading.body:
This paper presents consensus recommendations from more than 200 stakeholders on validation, certification, and national safety reporting for AI-enabled clinical decision support.

A 200-plus-stakeholder consensus process is a different kind of evidence than a single research study. It reflects what a broad cross-section of the field currently agrees should happen, which is useful for a governance audit even though it is not itself empirical proof that the recommended validation and certification processes reduce harm.

The paper does not report whether any health system has yet implemented the specific certification and reporting processes it recommends, only that the recommendations were agreed upon.

explain_beginner: Doctors increasingly use AI tools to help make medical decisions, but we need safeguards to ensure these tools work fairly and safely. Over 200 experts, including doctors, engineers, and patients, met to identify problems and suggest solutions. They recommended four main steps: building trustworthy systems from the start, testing and certifying AI tools before hospitals use them, creating a national system to report problems when they occur, and training doctors properly. This matters because getting AI right in healthcare can save lives, but getting it wrong could harm patients.
explain_business: Healthcare organizations implementing AI for clinical decisions face regulatory uncertainty and liability risks. This paper provides a roadmap for managing those risks: establish internal validation processes before deployment, maintain continuous monitoring systems to detect problems, and invest in staff training and clear documentation. Organizations that adopt these recommendations early can demonstrate responsible AI governance to regulators and stakeholders, potentially gaining competitive advantage. The recommendations also suggest future national safety reporting standards, which executives should anticipate when planning AI investments in clinical settings.
explain_practitioner: This consensus study brought together 200 stakeholders through webinars and a workshop to develop recommendations for AI-enabled clinical decision support systems. Through qualitative analysis and iterative consensus-building, the group identified four key areas: designing systems with safety and trustworthiness as core principles, establishing validation and certification protocols before deployment, implementing national-level safety monitoring and adverse event reporting mechanisms, and requiring comprehensive documentation and end-user training. The recommendations address critical gaps in current practices around explainability, fairness, model governance, and regulatory oversight needed for responsible clinical AI integration.
